ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in Figure A, within the horizontal plane of $x O y$, two parallel metal straight rails with a spacing of $l$ are fixed. A resistor with a resistance of $R$ is connected between them, and the two ends of the resistor are connected to an oscilloscope (with infinite internal resistance), which dynamically displays the voltage across the resistor $R$. A uniform magnetic field of magnitude $B$ exists between the two rails, with its direction perpendicular to the plane of the rails. At $t=0$, a conductor rod with mass $m$ and length $l$ starts to perform simple harmonic motion under the action of an external force $F$ along the $x$-axis from the position $x{=}-x_{0}$, with the equilibrium position at the origin $O$. The oscilloscope displays a sinusoidal curve of voltage versus time, as shown in Figure B. Friction and other resistances are negligible, and the conductor rod always moves perpendicular to the rails. (Hint: The area under the $F{-}x$ graph can represent the work done by the force $F$.)

1. What is the law of variation of the ampere force $F_{A}$ acting on the conductor rod with respect to time $t$?
2. What is the impulse of the external force \( F \) and the work done by the external force \( F \) during the time interval \( 0-0.25T \)?
3. If the period formula for simple harmonic motion is $T=2\pi{\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}}$ ($k$ is the restoring coefficient, $m$ is the mass of the conductor rod), then what is the relationship that $x_{0}$, $l$, $T$, $B$, and $U_{m}$ should satisfy?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In Figure A, two parallel metal guide rails are placed along the horizontal direction, the positive direction of the x-axis is marked on the right side, and the y-axis is marked vertically upward; the conductor rod is located to the left of the origin O, at the position marked x=-x0, and the external force F on the rod points in the +x direction; a resistor R is connected across the left side and is connected in parallel with the oscilloscope. In Figure B, the U-t graph displayed by the oscilloscope is a sine curve: when t=0, U=0; at 0.25T it reaches the positive peak value Um; at 0.5T it returns to 0; at 0.75T it reaches -Um; at T it returns to 0. Then reason: From Figure B, the oscilloscope voltage can be taken as U(t)=Um sin(ωt), where ω=2π/T. The internal resistance of the oscilloscope is infinitely large, so the current through resistor R is I=U/R. The magnitude of the induced electromotive force generated by the conductor rod cutting magnetic induction lines satisfies U=Blv, therefore v=U/(Bl)=Um sin(ωt)/(Bl). The direction of the ampere force always hinders the motion of the conductor rod, so F_A=-BIl=-(Bl/R)U, namely F_A(t)=-(BlUm/R)sin(2πt/T). Within 0 to T/4, v(0)=0, v(T/4)=Um/(Bl), so the change in momentum Δp=mUm/(Bl). The impulse of the ampere force is J_A=∫_0^{T/4} F_A dt=-(BlUm/R)∫_0^{T/4} sin(2πt/T)dt=-(BlUm/R)(T/2π). From the impulse theorem J_F+J_A=Δp, the impulse of the external force F is J_F=Δp-J_A=mUm/(Bl)+BlUmT/(2πR), with direction along the +x direction. The work done by the ampere force W_A=∫F_A v dt=-∫_0^{T/4} U^2/R dt=-(Um^2/R)∫_0^{T/4}sin^2(2πt/T)dt=-Um^2T/(8R). The change in kinetic energy ΔK=1/2 m[Um/(Bl)]^2. From the kinetic energy theorem W_F+W_A=ΔK, obtain W_F=ΔK-W_A=mUm^2/(2B^2l^2)+Um^2T/(8R). The simple harmonic motion starts from x=-x0 and reaches the equilibrium position O at T/4, when the velocity is maximum. The maximum velocity vmax=ωx0, and at the same time from electromagnetic induction there is vmax=Um/(Bl). Therefore x0=Um/(Blω)=TUm/(2πBl).
